credulity

/kruh-DOO-lih-tee/ - the stress falls on DOO · noun

Hear It

What It Means

Credulity means a readiness to believe things without proof.

Online quizzes that promise to reveal your true personality thrive on the credulity of readers who never ask how a dozen questions could know them.

Example

When the text message claimed her streaming account was locked and a small fee would restore it, Gran typed in her card number without a moment's doubt. It was not foolishness - she was sharp at cards and crosswords - but a lifetime of trusting official-looking letters had left her with a credulity that scammers count on.

Credulity is not the same as stupidity, and it is not quite trust either. It names one specific habit: accepting claims without asking for proof. Gran's mind is quick; what she lacks is the reflex to demand evidence before believing.

Compare the words

Synonyms · words with a similar meaning

trustfulness: Trustfulness is a warm readiness to rely on people - you assume your neighbor, your teammate, your doctor means well. Credulity aims at claims rather than people: swallowing the statement itself, however unlikely, without asking for proof. You trust a person; credulity accepts a story.

naivety: Naivety is broad inexperience of how the world works, and it shows everywhere - overpaying, oversharing, missing the joke. Credulity is one narrow habit inside that territory: accepting claims without demanding evidence. A naive person may misjudge anything; credulity specifically believes too easily.

faith: Faith is belief held without proof on purpose - a chosen, often deeply considered commitment to a person, a cause, or a religion. Credulity is not chosen at all: it is the unthinking habit of believing whatever comes along, because asking for evidence never occurs to you.

What it isn’t · antonyms and near-opposites

skepticism: the habit of demanding proof

wariness: guarded caution toward whatever is offered

Where it sits · how little proof belief demands

trust → credulity → gullibility

trust vs. credulity: Trust is usually earned by a person's track record; credulity goes further, handing out belief before any record exists.

gullibility vs. credulity: Gullibility goes a step past credulity: the credulous believe too easily, while the gullible actually get taken in and duped by it.

Build the Word

The pieces

Root — cred-: to believe (Latin credere)

Suffix — -ul-: inclined to

Suffix — -ity: state of being

Put it together: Cred- (Latin credere, 'to believe') + -ul- (inclined to) + -ity (the state of being) = the state of being inclined to believe. English keeps the adjective credulous, so credulity is the state of being credulous - and the same believing root runs through credit (a lender believes you will pay), creed (what a group believes), and incredible (impossible to believe).

Use the root in a new word: incredible: The escape artist saved the truly incredible trick for the final minute of the show.

Root Check

Word Choice

formal / literary

Credulity is the writer's word for believing too easily; it judges the habit, not the person's intelligence. Gullibility is blunter and more insulting - it implies someone will be fooled. Say a scam 'preys on credulity' in an essay; tell a friend they are 'too trusting' to their face.
